title: Taking Lives
full_review:
An FBI profiler learns the dangers of mixing business with pleasure in the better-than-average thriller "Taking Lives" (Warner Bros.). Despite a predictable plot and cookie-cutter creepiness, director D.J. Caruso keeps the action briskly paced and viewers on the edge of their seats.

A brief but gruesome prologue which takes place in Quebec in 1983 sets the stage by showing how the serial killer (around whom the ensuing investigation revolves) launched his bloody career. After an opening-credit montage of newspaper headlines and police reports chronicles his growing resume of death, the film flashes forward to the present, where a partially decomposed body is unearthed by a Montreal construction crew.

Enter Illeana Scott (Angelina Jolie), an FBI special agent reluctantly called in by the Canadian police chief (Tcheky Karyo) to help solve the case, which he feels is related to a string of unsolved homicides stretching back 20 years. Scott doesn't rely on traditional crime-solving techniques when trying to unravel the mysteries of a murderous mind, but opts for a more intuitive approach. Her unorthodox methodology ruffles those of the misogynistic cops (Oliver Martinez and Jean-Hughes Anglade) assigned to the case.

Of course Scott's all-work-and-no-play attitude leaves her little time for a social life -- which is just as well, since her idea of relaxation is cozying up over a glass of merlot and a file of grisly crime scene photos. But her stoic hull springs a leak when she becomes emotionally involved with an artist, James Costa (Ethan Hawke), who stumbled across the elusive psycho in action and, as an eyewitness, is now in danger of becoming the killer's next victim.

The script, based on a novel by Michael Pye, follows a pretty cut-and-dried formula, with much of the eerie moodiness supplied by standard-issue "Silence of the Lambs" atmospherics, including the requisite dark and dank killer's lair furnished in appropriately lurid decor. Still, Caruso navigates a potential minefield of cliches with skill, crafting an involving catch-him-before-he-kills-again screamer that is both stylish and suspenseful. However, with about 30 minutes left on the clock, Caruso derails the taut narrative, steering it into more conventional waters. The hokey final half-hour has a tacked-on feel and undoes much of the smart storytelling leading up to it.

Gena Rowlands lends her presence as the serial killer's imperious mother, who warns the police about the danger her deranged son poses and who fills in some of the blanks about his tortured childhood. The information she provides helps Scott develop the linchpin theory that not only helps her crack the case but also helps set up the film's big surprise plot twist. Without revealing too much, Scott determines that the murderer is "life-jacking," that is, stealing the identities of his victims. Kiefer Sutherland trolls the shadows of Montreal as the mystery man who matches Costa's description.

Jolie and Hawke are both in fine form, though much of the starlet's performance involves little more than slow-motion close-ups of her lush lips or of her feline eyes scanning for clues. Unlike the multilayered Clarice Starling in "The Silence of the Lambs," Scott's dispassionate demeanor and lack of substantial back story makes it difficult for viewers to invest the same level of emotion in her that they did in Jodie Foster's characterization. Of course, most characters in these types of cat-and-mouse films are not so much personalities as they are pieces in the overall narrative puzzle.

Morally speaking, the movie is a mixed bag. While not without some graphically disturbing images, Caruso deserves credit for showing a modicum of restraint in fashioning what could have been a much gorier and intensely violent film. However, he also includes a steamy sex scene that, though brief, is unnecessarily risque.

Still, while the level of filmmaking is a few cuts below "The Silence of the Lambs" in terms of character and story development, "Taking Lives" stops short of asking viewers to embrace its mass murderer as an anti-hero, as was the case with the depraved but debonair Hannibal Lecter. And though, admittedly, the film is more concerned with eliciting screams than sociological discussion, it does offer the devastating effects of childhood alienation as a means of explaining -- though not justifying -- the horrible crimes committed. In that way it is as much a why-dunit as it is a whodunit.

Due to recurring gory violence and associated autopsy images, a sexual encounter with partial nudity, and frequent rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
